final_method_items.reason: Best overall fix location among the candidates. This is the main declaration-finalization routine, and the bug is triggered by a local variable declaration with decltype(auto) and an initializer. It explicitly handles auto/decltype(auto) deduction, template-sensitive behavior, deferred initialization, and ties together initializer processing with deduction. The observed failure pattern—template + decltype(auto) + later wrong constant-expression check—fits very well with a bug in how this function preserves or replays the initializer tree for deduction.

C++0x [expr.const] used to say 6 An expression is a potential constant expression if it is a constant expression where all occurrences of function parameters are replaced by arbitrary constant expressions of the appropriate type. 2 A conditional expression is a constant expression unless it involves one of the following as a potentially evaluated subexpression (3.2), but subexpressions of logical AND (5.14), logical OR (5.15), and conditional (5.16) operations that are not evaluated are not considered.
final_method_items.reason: Extremely relevant because the actual emitted error is a bogus constant-expression diagnostic. This routine is the core checker that would produce that classification. The failure likely involves valid STMT_EXPR being sent here in the wrong context during template-body replay. It may not be the original source of the bad context, but it is one of the strongest places where a targeted fix or guard against this misclassification could live.

final_method_items.reason: Among the listed candidates, this is the strongest fix location. The reproducer hinges on a GNU statement expression used as the preserved initializer for `decltype(auto)`, and the bug appears only when optimization-related lowering/debug-frontier paths are taken. Gimplification is exactly where language-specific expression trees are transformed for later passes, so mishandling a statement-expression tree here could easily lose or corrupt semantic context, causing later template-body reprocessing to think the expression is in a constant-expression context. Although the true bug could also live in C++-specific decltype/template code not listed here, this is the best match among the available methods because it is closest to the critical transition from front-end trees to optimization/debug-sensitive internal form.

Very plausible because it is the template entry point for instantiating non-dependent expressions while temporarily clearing processing_template_decl. That matches the reproducer's template-only behavior. If the preserved decltype(auto) initializer containing STMT_EXPR is re-instantiated under the wrong flags/context here, GCC could wrongly run constant-expression checks and emit the -Wtemplate-body diagnostic.

final_method_items.summary: Obfuscate EXPR if it looks like an id-expression or member access so that the call to finish_decltype in do_auto_deduction will give the right result. If EVEN_UNEVAL, do this even in unevaluated context.
final_method_items.reason: Highly plausible because this function is explicitly part of the decltype(auto)-specific path: it rewrites or wraps the initializer expression so finish_decltype/do_auto_deduction see the right expression form. The reproducer differs only for decltype(auto) versus auto, which strongly points to this exact preservation machinery. If a STATEMENT_EXPR is wrapped incorrectly here, later template-body reprocessing could mis-handle it and trigger the bogus constant-expression diagnostic.

behavior_items: The reproducer uses GNU statement expressions, i.e. `({ ... })`, in two nested places: an outer statement expression that forms a full statement, and an inner statement expression `({3;})` that yields the value `3`. This is a GNU C/C++ extension rather than standard C++ syntax.

Inside the function template `fn`, the declaration `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` asks GCC to deduce the declared type of `v` from the initializer expression exactly as `decltype(initializer)` would. Because the initializer is a statement expression, the front end must preserve and analyze the exact expression form while deducing the type.

The nearby control case `auto v = ({3;});` behaves differently semantically: plain `auto` performs template-style type deduction from the initializer's type/value category rather than `decltype`-style deduction from the initializer expression form. That distinction matters to GCC's internal handling.

The non-template function `fn2` contains the same `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` pattern but compiles successfully, showing that the bad diagnosis depends on template processing or template-body checking rather than the construct being inherently invalid.

At `-O0`, the template version also compiles, so the source is accepted when optimization-related compiler paths are not active. This indicates the failure is not a normal semantic rejection of the code.

At `-O1`, GCC emits `error: statement-expression in a constant expression [-Wtemplate-body]` at the inner `({3;})` only for the `decltype(auto)` declaration in the template. That diagnostic is spurious because the code is not trying to form a constant expression there; it is only deducing a local variable type from a runtime expression.

The `[-Wtemplate-body]` tag is a clue that GCC is diagnosing something while reprocessing or validating a template body, likely during deferred analysis of dependent contexts. The compiler incorrectly concludes that the statement expression is being checked under constant-expression rules.

The bug report title mentions `gstatement-frontiers`, which is a debug-information setting/path in GCC. The observed optimization sensitivity implies that enabling optimization causes GCC to take a different internal path for bookkeeping/debug-frontier generation, and along that path the statement expression in the `decltype(auto)` initializer is misclassified.

The regression range noted in the report—works in GCC 10.5, fails starting in GCC 11.1 through trunk—suggests a front-end/internal representation change introduced after GCC 10 that altered how `decltype(auto)` initializers involving statement expressions are preserved or revisited.

The reproducer is carefully minimized to isolate three dimensions of behavior: `decltype(auto)` versus `auto`, template versus non-template, and `-O0` versus `-O1`. Only the combination `template + decltype(auto) + optimization-related path` fails, which strongly localizes the bug to compiler internals rather than language rules.

Semantically, the inner statement expression `({3;})` should simply have type `int` and prvalue category, so `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` should deduce `v` as `int`. There is no requirement for compile-time evaluation, and no rule in GNU C++ that forbids using a statement expression here.

The outer statement expression `({ decltype(auto) v = ({3;}); });` is largely incidental as a compact way to keep the declaration inside an expression statement. It exercises GCC's handling of nested statement expressions and local declarations, which may be relevant because the front end must track scopes and expression contexts precisely.

Because the same inner expression works with `auto`, the issue likely lies specifically in the code path that computes `decltype(auto)` by retaining the original initializer expression tree. That retained tree is then mishandled later under optimization/debug-frontier processing, producing an erroneous constant-expression check.

The report also notes that the issue can appear in non-template code in some circumstances, meaning the template form here is a reliable trigger but not necessarily the only manifestation. The essential exercised behavior is miscompilation of front-end semantic checks when optimization/debug-info related passes revisit `decltype(auto)` initializers containing GNU statement expressions.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer targets a GCC front-end regression involving GNU statement expressions used as initializers for `decltype(auto)`. The code itself is valid: `({3;})` yields an `int`, so `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` should deduce `v` as `int`. The minimized test shows that `auto` works, the same `decltype(auto)` form works in a non-template function, and everything works at `-O0`. The failure appears only when GCC takes the optimization-related internal path (`-O1`, and per the report tied to `gstatement-frontiers`/debug-info handling), where the template-body machinery incorrectly treats the statement expression as if it were being checked as a constant expression and emits the bogus `statement-expression in a constant expression [-Wtemplate-body]` error. In short, the reproducer exercises a regression in GCC's handling of `decltype(auto)` + statement expressions, exposed by template processing and optimization/debug-frontier internals, not by invalid source code.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is highly specific: valid GNU statement expressions used as the initializer of a local `decltype(auto)` declaration are accepted at `-O0`, accepted in the analogous `auto` case, and accepted in the non-template control case, but rejected in the template case once the optimization/debug-related path is enabled. That combination strongly indicates a GCC front-end regression rather than a language-rule violation. The key commonality is that `decltype(auto)` preserves the original initializer expression tree for exact `decltype`-style deduction, unlike plain `auto`, and that preserved tree contains a GNU statement-expression node. Later, during template-body rechecking or deferred processing triggered only on the optimized/debug-frontier path, GCC appears to revisit that initializer in the wrong semantic context and erroneously applies constant-expression restrictions, producing `statement-expression in a constant expression [-Wtemplate-body]`. The bug is therefore most likely in the C++ front end's handling of `decltype(auto)` initializer trees involving statement expressions when template bodies are deferred/reprocessed, especially where optimization/debug-info code changes statement frontiers, location/context bookkeeping, or forces secondary semantic validation. Since GCC 10.5 worked and GCC 11.1+ fails, the likely defect was introduced by a regression in how such expressions are preserved, wrapped, or re-instantiated across template processing and optimization/debug-info integration.
possible_causes: Incorrect C++ front-end handling of `decltype(auto)` deduction from a GNU statement-expression initializer, where the preserved initializer tree is later re-evaluated under `constexpr`/constant-expression rules during template-body checking.

A bug in deferred template processing or template instantiation replay that loses the original non-constant-evaluation context for statement expressions inside `decltype(auto)` initializers, leading to a spurious `-Wtemplate-body` diagnostic.

Regression in the code path that distinguishes `auto` deduction from `decltype(auto)` deduction: `auto` may use only the deduced type, while `decltype(auto)` retains the full expression, and that retained expression is mishandled when it is a `STATEMENT_EXPR` node.

Misclassification of GNU statement-expression trees as needing constant-expression validation when optimization/debug-info related processing revisits expression frontiers or declaration initializers.

A bug in `gstatement-frontiers`/debug location frontier generation that perturbs front-end bookkeeping for nested statement expressions, causing the initializer to be rewrapped or reanalyzed in an invalid semantic context.

Incorrect scope/context restoration for nested statement expressions inside local declarations during template-body validation, so the inner `({3;})` is checked as if it appeared in a forbidden immediate/constant context.

Front-end regression introduced after GCC 10 in cp/ tree handling for `decltype(auto)` declarations, possibly involving stripping or preserving references/value category from statement expressions and accidentally routing them through constant-expression diagnostics.
An optimization-enabled early or secondary semantic pass that touches debug-boundary statements and erroneously calls constant-expression checking on decltype deduction operands within templates.

Improper TREE_CONSTANT / potential_constant_expression marking or propagation for statement-expression nodes inside `decltype(auto)` initializers, causing later template diagnostics to believe the code is participating in constant evaluation.

A mismatch between parser/semantic acceptance of GNU statement expressions and later template-body warning/error machinery, where valid extension nodes are accepted initially but rejected when the body is reprocessed under optimization-sensitive paths.
evidence: `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` fails but `auto v = ({3;});` succeeds, isolating the issue to the exact-expression preservation path used by `decltype(auto)` rather than general type deduction.
The same `decltype(auto)` construct succeeds in non-template `fn2`, so the construct itself is valid and the failure depends on template-body processing.
The failure occurs at `-O1` but not at `-O0`, showing it is triggered by an optimization/debug-related internal path rather than normal parsing or semantic analysis.

The emitted diagnostic is `statement-expression in a constant expression [-Wtemplate-body]`, which is inconsistent with the source semantics and points to an erroneous constant-expression check during template-body reprocessing.
The report explicitly mentions `gstatement-frontiers`, tying the regression to debug/frontier machinery that can alter how statements/expressions are revisited under optimization.
The inner GNU statement expression `({3;})` should simply yield `int`; there is no language requirement for constant evaluation in this initializer, so the diagnostic is necessarily spurious.
The regression range—works in GCC 10.5, fails from GCC 11.1 onward—supports a specific front-end/internal representation regression rather than intended language behavior.
Only the combination `template + decltype(auto) + optimization/debug-related path` fails, a classic signature of incorrect deferred semantic reanalysis or context propagation in the compiler.

selected_files.reason: Most suspicious because this is where C++ parsing/semantic actions are shared between normal parsing and template instantiation, and the bug is specifically about a valid `decltype(auto)` initializer with nested GNU statement expressions being reprocessed in the wrong context only for template bodies. The `-Wtemplate-body` diagnostic strongly suggests deferred/template-body semantic checking is misclassifying the preserved initializer expression as subject to constant-expression rules.

Very likely involved because `decltype(auto) v = ({3;});` is a local variable declaration, and `decl.cc` owns major logic for variable declarations, initializer checking, and `decltype(auto)` deduction setup in the C++ front end. The distinction between `auto` working and `decltype(auto)` failing points to declaration-specific handling of the initializer tree being wrong for the latter.

High suspicion due to the template-only trigger and the `[-Wtemplate-body]` marker. This file handles deferred templates, pending instantiations, and replay of template bodies; a bug here could easily cause a preserved statement-expression initializer used for `decltype(auto)` deduction to be revisited under an invalid constant-evaluation or diagnostic context.

Plausible because statement expressions and decltype-style deduction ultimately depend on expression typing and value-category preservation. Since `decltype(auto)` relies on the exact initializer expression rather than the simpler deduction path used by `auto`, any regression in expression type/value-category handling for `STATEMENT_EXPR` nodes could surface here.

The emitted error is explicitly about 'statement-expression in a constant expression', which should not apply here. Even if this file is not the root cause, it is a likely place where an incorrect constant-expression check is being invoked on the initializer during template-body reanalysis, especially after a context propagation bug elsewhere.

The bug report explicitly mentions `gstatement-frontiers`, which is closely related to statement frontier/discriminator/debug bookkeeping built around CFG construction. Since the failure is optimization-sensitive and tied to debug/frontier machinery, this file is a plausible bridge where statement/frontier processing perturbs later semantic rechecking or location/context tracking.

Optimization plus debug-info sensitivity makes this a candidate, since var-tracking is a major debug-related pass activated on optimized code paths. While it should not affect front-end semantics, regressions involving debug bookkeeping sometimes expose latent tree/context mishandling, especially around local declarations and statement boundaries.

GNU statement expressions are a language-extension construct that need special lowering/gimplification support. Because the reproducer depends on nested statement expressions and only appears once optimization-related lowering paths are active, mishandling of statement-expression trees during genericization/gimplification is a credible contributing source.

Also suspicious for the optimization-only aspect: if the preserved initializer expression for `decltype(auto)` is transformed differently once gimplification is involved, a malformed or rewrapped tree could later trigger the bogus constant-expression diagnostic. This is less C++-specific than `cp/*` files, but consistent with the optimization/debug-path dependency.

Least suspicious among the selected files, but still relevant because the report indicates `-O1` triggers the bug even when toggling listed optimization flags does not isolate it. That suggests a pass-pipeline or early-pass enablement difference, and this file controls pass scheduling that could activate the problematic template/debug-frontier interaction.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of them throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. DECLSPECS and DECLARATOR are the parts of the declaration; they describe the function's name and the type it returns, but twisted together in a fashion that parallels the syntax of C. FLAGS is a bitwise or of SF_PRE_PARSED (indicating that the DECLARATOR is really the DECL for the function we are about to process and that DECLSPECS should be ignored), SF_INCLASS_INLINE indicating that the function is an inline defined in-class. For example, "class A local_a(1,2);" means that variable local_a is an aggregate of type A, which should have a constructor applied to it with the argument list [1, 2]. On entry, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) should be NULL_TREE or error_mark_node, or may be a BLOCK if the function has been defined previously in this translation unit. On exit, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) will be error_mark_node if the function has never been defined, or a BLOCK if the function has been defined somewhere.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: tree check_explicit_specialization (tree declarator, tree decl, int template_count, int flags, tree attrlist)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Check to see if the function just declared, as indicated in DECLARATOR, and in DECL, is a specialization of a function template. We may also discover that the declaration is an explicit instantiation at this point. Returns DECL, or an equivalent declaration that should be used instead if all goes well. Issues an error message if something is amiss. Returns error_mark_node if the error is not easily recoverable. FLAGS is a bitmask consisting of the following flags: 2: The function has a definition. 4: The function is a friend. The TEMPLATE_COUNT is the number of references to qualifying template classes that appeared in the name of the function. Returns 0 if the type deduction succeeds, 1 otherwise. The parameter STRICT is a bitwise or of the following flags: UNIFY_ALLOW_NONE: Require an exact match between PARM and ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_MORE_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be more cv-qualified (by qualification conversion) than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_LESS_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be less cv-qualified than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_DERIVED: Allow the deduced ARG to be a template base class of ARG, or a pointer to a template base class of the type pointed to by ARG. Note that DECL can be defined in this translation unit, if required.

The 1998 std underspecified function template partial ordering, and DR214 addresses the issue. We take pairs of arguments, one from each of the templates, and deduce them against each other. One of the templates will be more specialized if all the *other* template's arguments deduce against its arguments and at least one of its arguments *does* *not* deduce against the other template's corresponding argument. Deduction is done as for class templates. The arguments used in deduction have reference and top level cv qualifiers removed. Iff both arguments were originally reference types *and* deduction succeeds in both directions, an lvalue reference wins against an rvalue reference and otherwise the template with the more cv-qualified argument wins for that pairing (if neither is more cv-qualified, they both are equal). gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: TEMPLATES is a TREE_LIST. Each TREE_VALUE is a TEMPLATE_DECL. Return the TREE_LIST node with the most specialized template, if any. If there is no most specialized template, the error_mark_node is returned. Note that this function does not look at, or modify, the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of any of the nodes. Since the node returned is one of the elements of INSTANTIATIONS, callers may store information in the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of the nodes, and retrieve it from the value returned.

If DECL is a specialization of some template, return the most general such template. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE. For example, given: template <class T> struct S { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int>::f(U)' this will return the full template. This function will not trace past partial specializations, however. For example, given in addition: template <class T> struct S<T*> { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int*>::f(U)' this will return `template <class T> template <class U> S<T*>::f(U)'.

Return the most specialized of the template partial specializations which can produce TARGET, a specialization of some class or variable template. The value returned is actually a TREE_LIST; the TREE_VALUE is a TEMPLATE_DECL node corresponding to the partial specialization, while the TREE_PURPOSE is the set of template arguments that must be substituted into the template pattern in order to generate TARGET. If the choice of partial specialization is ambiguous, a diagnostic is issued, and the error_mark_node is returned. If there are no partial specializations matching TARGET, then NULL_TREE is returned, indicating that the primary template should be used.

TMPL should be the template into which tsubst'ing should occur for DECL, not the most general template. One reason for doing this is a scenario like this: template <class T> void f(const T&, int i); void g() { f(3, 7); } template <class T> void f(const T& t, const int i) { } Note that when the template is first instantiated, with instantiate_template, the resulting DECL will have no name for the first parameter, and the wrong type for the second. Similarly, if a pointer type Y * ... exceptions of type Y * or that are pointers to any type publicly and unambiguously derived from Y. Otherwise a function only allows exceptions that have the same type ..." This does not mention cv qualifiers and is different to what throw [except.throw] and catch [except.catch] will do. While expanding variables, we may encounter recursion cycles because of mutual (possibly indirect) dependencies between two particular variables (or values), say A and B. If we're trying to expand A when we get to B, which in turn attempts to expand A, if we can't find any other expansion for B, we'll add B to this pending-recursion stack, and tentatively return NULL for its location. This tentative value will be used for any other occurrences of B, unless A gets some other location, in which case it will notify B that it is worth another try at computing a location for it, and it will use the location computed for A then. At the end of the expansion, the tentative NULL locations become final for all members of PENDING that didn't get a notification. This function performs this finalization of NULL locations.

If its type is different from its canonical type, wrap the whole thing inside a NOP_EXPR and force the type of the COMPONENT_REF to be the canonical type. The canonical type of a COMPONENT_REF is the type of the field being referenced--unless the field is a bit-field which can be read directly in a smaller mode, in which case the canonical type is the sign-appropriate type corresponding to that mode.

Gimplify a CLEANUP_POINT_EXPR. Currently this works by adding GIMPLE_WITH_CLEANUP_EXPRs to the prequeue as we encounter cleanups while gimplifying the body, and converting them to TRY_FINALLY_EXPRs when we return to this function. FIXME should we complexify the prequeue handling instead? Or use flags for all the cleanups and let the optimizer tighten them up? The current code seems pretty fragile; it will break on a cleanup within any non-conditional nesting. But any such nesting would be broken, anyway; we can't write a TRY_FINALLY_EXPR that starts inside a nesting construct and continues out of it. We can do that at the RTL level, though, so having an optimizer to tighten up try/finally regions would be a Good Thing.

gcc/gimplify.cc.summary: Convert the GENERIC expression tree *EXPR_P to GIMPLE. If the expression produces a value to be used as an operand inside a GIMPLE statement, the value will be stored back in *EXPR_P. This value will be a tree of class tcc_declaration, tcc_constant, tcc_reference or an SSA_NAME. The corresponding sequence of GIMPLE statements is emitted in PRE_P and POST_P. Additionally, this process may overwrite parts of the input expression during gimplification. Ideally, it should be possible to do non-destructive gimplification. EXPR_P points to the GENERIC expression to convert to GIMPLE. If the expression needs to evaluate to a value to be used as an operand in a GIMPLE statement, this value will be stored in EXPR_P on exit. This happens when the caller specifies one of fb_lvalue or fb_rvalue fallback flags. PRE_P will contain the sequence of GIMPLE statements corresponding to the evaluation of EXPR and all the side-effects that must be executed before the main expression. On exit, the last statement of PRE_P is the core statement being gimplified. For instance, when gimplifying 'if (++a)' the last statement in PRE_P will be 'if (t.1)' where t.1 is the result of pre-incrementing 'a'. POST_P

related_methods.reason: This method is explicitly involved in making decltype deduction see the original expression form correctly: its comment says it obfuscates EXPR so that finish_decltype in do_auto_deduction gives the right result. The reproducer fails only for decltype(auto), not auto, and only when the initializer is a GNU statement-expression. That strongly points to the decltype(auto)-specific expression-preservation path, where a STATEMENT_EXPR may be wrapped or transformed incorrectly and later rechecked in the wrong constant-expression/template-body context.

This is the routine that finishes a GNU statement-expression and returns the expression node representing it. Since the bogus diagnostic specifically targets the inner ({3;}) and the bug report mentions nested statement expressions plus optimization/debug-frontier sensitivity, an incorrect tree shape, flags, or context on the resulting statement-expression node here could easily cause later template-body processing to misclassify it as being in constant-evaluation.

Most suspicious because this is the main declaration-finalization path for variables and explicitly handles installing the initializer, decltype(auto)-style variable completion, and template-sensitive initialization state. The bug is triggered specifically by a local variable declaration with initializer `({3;})`, and the spurious `[-Wtemplate-body]` constant-expression diagnostic suggests the initializer is being finalized or replayed in the wrong semantic context here.

Directly verifies a declaration initializer and records it on the declaration. Since the failure hinges on `decltype(auto)` preserving the exact initializer expression tree, this routine is a strong candidate for incorrectly classifying a GNU statement-expression initializer, or routing it through constant-expression/template-body checking during deferred processing.

Most suspicious because the bug looks like a template-only reprocessing/instantiation error where a non-dependent initializer expression retained for decltype(auto) is revisited in the wrong semantic context. This helper explicitly performs substitution after the caller has cleared processing_template_decl, so a regression here could easily cause a statement-expression initializer to be reanalyzed as if constant-evaluated or otherwise outside its original context, matching the spurious -Wtemplate-body diagnostic.

Very relevant because the failure occurs during template-body checking on an expression that should be accepted, and this routine is the front-end entry point for instantiating non-dependent expressions in template machinery. If decltype(auto) preserves the original STATEMENT_EXPR tree and this path instantiates or checks it under the wrong flags/context, it would explain why only the template + decltype(auto) case fails while the non-template case succeeds.

Most suspicious because the reproducer centers on initialization of a local variable with a GNU statement-expression, and this method specifically handles initialization semantics distinct from assignment. A regression in how it preserves or converts the initializer tree for `decltype(auto)` could cause the initializer to be revisited later in the wrong semantic context and spuriously treated as requiring constant-expression checking.

`decltype(auto)` versus `auto` is the key behavioral split in the reproducer, and this method controls the standard lvalue/rvalue/array/function decay behavior applied to expressions. If statement-expression operands are incorrectly decayed or normalized here for the `decltype(auto)` path, GCC could lose the exact expression/category information and later misclassify the preserved tree during template-body rechecking.

Most suspicious because the emitted diagnostic is specifically about treating the statement-expression as if it were in a constant-expression context, and this routine is the core checker that decides whether an expression is a potentially constant expression and issues diagnostics. The bug pattern strongly suggests the decltype(auto) initializer tree is being revisited here during template-body processing under the wrong context, producing the spurious [-Wtemplate-body] error on a GNU statement-expression.

Highly suspicious because the failure is template-sensitive and optimization-sensitive, and this routine explicitly folds non-dependent expressions in templates after full instantiation. A non-dependent statement-expression inside a decltype(auto) initializer could be incorrectly routed through constant-expression folding/checking here, especially on the optimized path that reprocesses template bodies.

Most suspicious because the bug report explicitly points at gstatement-frontiers/debug-frontier behavior under optimization, and this method is the one in this file that assigns location discriminators to basic blocks. A regression in discriminator assignment for nested statement-expression code could perturb source-location/frontier bookkeeping and trigger later front-end/template-body reprocessing in the wrong context.

Closely related to debug location handling: it computes discriminator values for shared source loci. The reproducer depends on optimization and debug-frontier-sensitive paths, so incorrect handling of repeated/nested loci from statement expressions could contribute to the spurious diagnostic by confusing location identity across blocks.

This is the top-level routine that finds variable locations for the whole function, exactly the kind of optimization/debug-info path implicated by the report's mention of gstatement-frontiers. Since the failure appears only with optimization-enabled debug-location processing, the main orchestration point of var-tracking is the most suspicious place for triggering or exposing the bad interaction.

The bug seems tied to statement frontiers and optimized debug bookkeeping within function bodies. This method computes per-basic-block changes of variable locations, so it is a central place where statement boundaries, location notes, and dataflow over optimized code are interpreted; a mistake here could plausibly cause later reprocessing in the wrong source context and lead to the spurious template-body diagnostic.

Most suspicious because the bug is optimization/debug-path sensitive and explicitly tied to gstatement-frontiers, which interacts with gimplification of language-specific expressions before later passes. reviewed_methods.signature: void cp_finish_decl (tree decl, tree init, bool init_const_expr_p, tree asmspec_tree, int flags)
reviewed_methods.summary: Finish processing of a declaration; install its line number and initial value. If the length of an array type is not known before, it must be determined now, from the initial value, or it is an error. INIT is the initializer (if any) for DECL. If INIT_CONST_EXPR_P is true, then INIT is an integral constant expression. FLAGS is LOOKUP_ONLYCONVERTING if the = init syntax was used, else 0 if the (init) syntax was used.
reviewed_methods.reason: Best overall fix location among the candidates. This is the main declaration-finalization routine, and the bug is triggered by a local variable declaration with decltype(auto) and an initializer. It explicitly handles auto/decltype(auto) deduction, template-sensitive behavior, deferred initialization, and ties together initializer processing with deduction. The observed failure pattern—template + decltype(auto) + later wrong constant-expression check—fits very well with a bug in how this function preserves or replays the initializer tree for deduction.

reviewed_methods.signature: static bool potential_constant_expression_1 (tree t, bool want_rval, bool strict, bool now, tsubst_flags_t flags, tree *jump_target)
reviewed_methods.summary: Return true if T denotes a potentially constant expression. Issue diagnostic as appropriate under control of FLAGS. If WANT_RVAL is true, an lvalue-rvalue conversion is implied. If NOW is true, we want to consider the expression in the current context, independent of constexpr substitution. C++0x [expr.const] used to say 6 An expression is a potential constant expression if it is a constant expression where all occurrences of function parameters are replaced by arbitrary constant expressions of the appropriate type. 2 A conditional expression is a constant expression unless it involves one of the following as a potentially evaluated subexpression (3.2), but subexpressions of logical AND (5.14), logical OR (5.15), and conditional (5.16) operations that are not evaluated are not considered.
reviewed_methods.reason: Extremely relevant because the actual emitted error is a bogus constant-expression diagnostic. This routine is the core checker that would produce that classification. The failure likely involves valid STMT_EXPR being sent here in the wrong context during template-body replay. It may not be the original source of the bad context, but it is one of the strongest places where a targeted fix or guard against this misclassification could live.

reviewed_methods.reason: Among the listed candidates, this is the strongest fix location. The reproducer hinges on a GNU statement expression used as the preserved initializer for `decltype(auto)`, and the bug appears only when optimization-related lowering/debug-frontier paths are taken. Gimplification is exactly where language-specific expression trees are transformed for later passes, so mishandling a statement-expression tree here could easily lose or corrupt semantic context, causing later template-body reprocessing to think the expression is in a constant-expression context. Although the true bug could also live in C++-specific decltype/template code not listed here, this is the best match among the available methods because it is closest to the critical transition from front-end trees to optimization/debug-sensitive internal form.

That matches the reproducer's template-only behavior. If the preserved decltype(auto) initializer containing STMT_EXPR is re-instantiated under the wrong flags/context here, GCC could wrongly run constant-expression checks and emit the -Wtemplate-body diagnostic.

reviewed_methods.signature: tree fold_non_dependent_expr (tree t, tsubst_flags_t complain , bool manifestly_const_eval , tree object )
reviewed_methods.summary: Like maybe_constant_value but first fully instantiate the argument. Note: this is equivalent to instantiate_non_dependent_expr_sfinae (t, complain) followed by maybe_constant_value but is more efficient, because it calls instantiation_dependent_expression_p and potential_constant_expression at most once. The manifestly_const_eval argument is passed to maybe_constant_value. Callers should generally pass their active complain, or if they are in a non-template, diagnosing context, they can use the default of tf_warning_or_error. Callers that might be within a template context, don't have a complain parameter, and aren't going to remember the result for long (e.g. null_ptr_cst_p), can pass tf_none and deal with error_mark_node appropriately.
reviewed_methods.reason: Strong candidate because it combines template-only behavior with non-dependent expression folding and potential constant-evaluation machinery. That aligns well with the reproducer's dependence on template-body processing and the spurious constant-expression path. Slightly less direct than cp_finish_decl and potential_constant_expression_1 because it is more of a dispatcher, but still a credible location for the wrong folding/checking decision.

reviewed_methods.signature: tree convert_for_initialization (tree exp, tree type, tree rhs, int flags, impl_conv_rhs errtype, tree fndecl, int parmnum, tsubst_flags_t complain)
reviewed_methods.summary: Convert RHS to be of type TYPE. If EXP is nonzero, it is the target of the initialization. ERRTYPE indicates what kind of error the implicit conversion is. Two major differences between the behavior of `convert_for_assignment' and `convert_for_initialization' are that references are bashed in the former, while copied in the latter, and aggregates are assigned in the former (operator=) while initialized in the latter (X(X&)). If using constructor make sure no conversion operator exists, if one does exist, an ambiguity exists.
reviewed_methods.reason: On the initialization path, but less likely than decl/semantics/template routines. The bug is not about conversion correctness of the initializer value; the statement expression has a simple int result and works with auto. The stronger signal is mis-preservation and later rechecking of the original expression form, which is upstream of ordinary conversion.

reviewed_methods.signature: tree decay_conversion (tree exp, tsubst_flags_t complain, bool reject_builtin )
reviewed_methods.summary: Perform the conversions in [expr] that apply when an lvalue appears in an rvalue context: the lvalue-to-rvalue, array-to-pointer, and function-to-pointer conversions. In addition, bitfield references are converted to their declared types. Note that this function does not perform the lvalue-to-rvalue conversion for class types. If you need that conversion for class types, then you probably need to use force_rvalue. Although the returned value is being used as an rvalue, this function does not wrap the returned expression in a NON_LVALUE_EXPR; the caller is expected to be mindful of the fact that the return value is no longer an lvalue.
reviewed_methods.reason: Possible only indirectly. The reproducer's key issue is exact decltype(auto) expression handling, where decay behavior is usually precisely what decltype(auto) avoids. Since auto succeeds and decltype(auto) fails, a generic decay conversion routine is a weaker match for the root cause than expression-preservation or template re-instantiation code.

The failure message strongly suggests the root bug is already baked in before this pass, so this is a weak primary fix location.

reviewed_methods.reason: This helper only allocates/increments discriminator numbers per source line. While discriminator handling is adjacent to the gstatement-frontiers theme, the routine is too small and generic to plausibly cause the specific regression involving `decltype(auto)` deduction, statement expressions, and template-body constant-expression rechecking. At most it would contribute indirectly to debug metadata quality, not front-end semantic misclassification.
